entries.meaning: Detailed examination of something; the result of that examination.
examples: Her analysis of the data took three weeks.
Both analyses reached the same conclusion.
Further analysis is needed.
The paper offers a careful analysis of the failure.
Independent analyses were commissioned from two firms.
In the final analysis, it came down to money.

senses.head: Detailed examination
examples: Her analysis of the data took three weeks.
Both analyses reached the same conclusion.
Further analysis is needed.

senses.head: A written or spoken account of that examination
examples: The paper offers a careful analysis of the failure.
Independent analyses were commissioned from two firms.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: In the final analysis, it came down to money.

entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as an activity
entries.contrast: ✗ analysises is wrong. Note also the verb analyze and the adjective analytical, which change the s to a z sound.

entries.meaning: The foundation or starting point for something.
examples: There is no basis for that accusation.
The bases of the two theories are quite different.
His argument has a solid factual basis.
She works there on a part-time basis.
Meetings are held on a monthly basis.
Employees are hired on a contract basis.

senses.head: A foundation or underlying reason
examples: There is no basis for that accusation.
The bases of the two theories are quite different.
His argument has a solid factual basis.

senses.head: A regular arrangement — on a … basis
body: Extremely common in business English. (на основе, на условиях)
examples: She works there on a part-time basis.
Meetings are held on a monthly basis.
Employees are hired on a contract basis.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the bases for the claim are weak
entries.contrast: Bases is the plural of both basis /ˈbeɪsiːz/ and base /ˈbeɪsɪz/ — a genuine ambiguity in writing, resolved only by sound or context. ✗ Basises is wrong.

entries.meaning: A time of intense difficulty or danger.
examples: The country faced its worst financial crisis in decades.
Two crises hit the company in the same quarter.
She handles a crisis better than anyone I know.
The fever broke and the crisis passed.
They set up a crisis hotline within a day.
Both crises were handled by the same team.

senses.head: A time of serious difficulty
examples: The country faced its worst financial crisis in decades.
Two crises hit the company in the same quarter.
She handles a crisis better than anyone I know.

senses.head: A turning point in an illness or situation
examples: The fever broke and the crisis passed.

senses.head: Attributive
examples: They set up a crisis hotline within a day.
Both crises were handled by the same team.

entries.contrast: ✗ crisises is wrong. The adjective is critical, from the same Greek root meaning 'to decide' — a crisis is originally the turning point at which a decision must be made.

entries.meaning: A statement put forward as a proposition; a long piece of academic writing.
examples: His central thesis is that the war was avoidable.
The two theses contradict each other.
She finished her master's thesis in April.
All theses are archived in the library.
He defends his thesis next month.
The argument moves from thesis to antithesis to synthesis.

senses.head: A proposition to be defended
examples: His central thesis is that the war was avoidable.
The two theses contradict each other.

senses.head: A long academic paper
examples: She finished her master's thesis in April.
All theses are archived in the library.
He defends his thesis next month.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: The argument moves from thesis to antithesis to synthesis.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both theses were defended
entries.contrast: ✗ thesises is wrong. In American universities a thesis is usually a master's project and a dissertation the doctoral one — the reverse of British usage.

entries.meaning: A proposed explanation, put forward to be tested.
examples: The hypothesis was not supported by the data.
Several competing hypotheses remain.
We tested each hypothesis independently.
Her hypothesis turned out to be right.
That's a reasonable working hypothesis.

senses.head: A testable proposal
examples: The hypothesis was not supported by the data.
Several competing hypotheses remain.
We tested each hypothesis independently.
Her hypothesis turned out to be right.

senses.head: A guess or assumption
examples: That's a reasonable working hypothesis.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the hypotheses were tested separately
entries.contrast: ✗ hypothesises is wrong. Note the stress falls on the second syllable in both forms. The adjective is hypothetical.

entries.meaning: Identification of an illness or a problem.
examples: The diagnosis took months to reach.
Both diagnoses pointed to the same condition.
She sought a second opinion on the diagnosis.
Early diagnosis improves survival dramatically.
The engineer's diagnosis was a failed sensor.

senses.head: Identification of a disease
examples: The diagnosis took months to reach.
Both diagnoses pointed to the same condition.
She sought a second opinion on the diagnosis.
Early diagnosis improves survival dramatically.

senses.head: Identification of any problem
examples: The engineer's diagnosis was a failed sensor.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the two diagnoses conflicted
entries.contrast: ✗ diagnosises is wrong. The verb is diagnose and the adjective diagnostic.

entries.meaning: A forecast of how an illness or situation will develop.
examples: The prognosis is good if treatment starts now.
Both prognoses were cautiously optimistic.
Doctors gave a poor prognosis.
The prognosis for the industry is bleak.
Analysts offered wildly different prognoses.

senses.head: A medical forecast
examples: The prognosis is good if treatment starts now.
Both prognoses were cautiously optimistic.
Doctors gave a poor prognosis.

senses.head: A forecast about anything
examples: The prognosis for the industry is bleak.
Analysts offered wildly different prognoses.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the prognoses were guarded
entries.contrast: A diagnosis says what is wrong; a prognosis says what will happen next. They are constantly confused.

entries.meaning: Special importance given to something; stress placed on a word.
examples: The school places great emphasis on writing.
The emphasis has shifted to prevention.
Different departments have different emphases.
Put the emphasis on the second syllable.
The italics indicate emphasis.

senses.head: Special importance or attention
examples: The school places great emphasis on writing.
The emphasis has shifted to prevention.
Different departments have different emphases.

senses.head: Stress on a syllable or word
examples: Put the emphasis on the second syllable.
The italics indicate emphasis.

entries.countability: countable, and uncountable in general use
entries.agreement: plural verb — the emphases differ between the two editions
entries.contrast: ✗ emphasises is wrong as a noun plural — emphasises is the British spelling of the verb emphasizes. Americans write emphasizes.

entries.meaning: A line about which something rotates, or a reference line on a graph.
examples: The Earth turns on its axis once a day.
The planet's axis is tilted 23 degrees.
Label both axes before you plot anything.
Time goes on the horizontal axis.
The vertical axis shows temperature.
The Axis powers signed the pact in 1940.

senses.head: A line of rotation
examples: The Earth turns on its axis once a day.
The planet's axis is tilted 23 degrees.

senses.head: A reference line on a graph
examples: Label both axes before you plot anything.
Time goes on the horizontal axis.
The vertical axis shows temperature.

senses.head: An alliance between countries
examples: The Axis powers signed the pact in 1940.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both axes are labeled
entries.contrast: Axes is also the plural of ax — but pronounced differently: AK-seez for axes of rotation, AK-siz for the chopping tools. In writing only context tells them apart.

entries.meaning: A fertile place in a desert; figuratively, any refuge.
examples: The caravan reached the oasis by nightfall.
Several oases lie along the old trade route.
Palm trees mark the oasis from miles away.
The garden is an oasis in the middle of the city.
Her office was an oasis of quiet.
These parks are oases for people with no yard.

senses.head: A watered place in a desert
examples: The caravan reached the oasis by nightfall.
Several oases lie along the old trade route.
Palm trees mark the oasis from miles away.

senses.head: A place of relief or calm
examples: The garden is an oasis in the middle of the city.
Her office was an oasis of quiet.
These parks are oases for people with no yard.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the oases are days apart
entries.contrast: ✗ oasises is wrong. Note the stress on the second syllable in both forms.

entries.meaning: A round bracket; also a word or phrase inserted as an aside.
examples: Put the date in parentheses.
Close the parenthesis after the citation.
The formula has three sets of parentheses.
The whole clause is a parenthesis and can be cut.
His speech was full of parentheses and digressions.

senses.head: The punctuation mark
body: Almost always plural, since they come in pairs. (скобка)
examples: Put the date in parentheses.
Close the parenthesis after the citation.
The formula has three sets of parentheses.

senses.head: An inserted aside
examples: The whole clause is a parenthesis and can be cut.
His speech was full of parentheses and digressions.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the parentheses are unbalanced
entries.contrast: In everyday American speech the punctuation marks are usually just called parens or round brackets. The singular refers to one mark, so a pair is always parentheses.

entries.meaning: The three dots marking omitted words; also the omission itself.
examples: Use an ellipsis to show you cut part of the quote.
The page is littered with ellipses.
"Coming?" is an ellipsis of "Are you coming?"
English allows ellipsis after auxiliary verbs.
Both ellipses make the sentence hard to parse.

senses.head: The punctuation mark
examples: Use an ellipsis to show you cut part of the quote.
The page is littered with ellipses.

senses.head: Omission of words that are understood
examples: "Coming?" is an ellipsis of "Are you coming?"
English allows ellipsis after auxiliary verbs.
Both ellipses make the sentence hard to parse.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the ellipses mark omitted text
entries.contrast: Ellipses is also the plural of ellipse, the oval shape — and the two are pronounced differently: ih-LIP-seez for both, in fact, which makes them true homophones distinguished only by context.

entries.meaning: A brief summary of a book, film, or argument.
examples: Send a one-page synopsis with the manuscript.
All the synopses were written by the same intern.
The synopsis gives away the ending.
He read the synopsis instead of the book.
Both synopses leave out the subplot.

senses.head: A summary
examples: Send a one-page synopsis with the manuscript.
All the synopses were written by the same intern.
The synopsis gives away the ending.
He read the synopsis instead of the book.
Both synopses leave out the subplot.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the synopses are one page each

entries.meaning: The combination of parts into a whole; in chemistry, the making of a compound.
examples: The book is a synthesis of thirty years of research.
Both syntheses draw on the same sources.
The synthesis takes four steps.
Several syntheses of the drug have been published.
Protein synthesis happens in the ribosome.

senses.head: A combining of ideas
examples: The book is a synthesis of thirty years of research.
Both syntheses draw on the same sources.

senses.head: In chemistry
examples: The synthesis takes four steps.
Several syntheses of the drug have been published.
Protein synthesis happens in the ribosome.

entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a process
entries.agreement: plural verb — the syntheses were repeated
entries.contrast: ✗ synthesises is wrong as a noun. The verb is synthesize.

entries.meaning: A relatively mild mental or emotional disturbance.
examples: The neurosis had built up over years.
Both neuroses trace back to the same event.
He writes about his neuroses with real humor.
Her neurosis about punctuality drives everyone crazy.
The whole industry runs on collective neuroses.

senses.head: The condition
examples: The neurosis had built up over years.
Both neuroses trace back to the same event.
He writes about his neuroses with real humor.

senses.head: Loosely — an anxious obsession
examples: Her neurosis about punctuality drives everyone crazy.
The whole industry runs on collective neuroses.

entries.agreement: plural verb — his neuroses are well documented
entries.contrast: No longer a formal clinical term, but common in everyday and literary use. Compare psychosis → psychoses, which is still clinical.

entries.meaning: A complete change of form; in biology, the transformation of a larva into an adult.
examples: The metamorphosis from caterpillar to butterfly takes two weeks.
Insect metamorphoses follow a fixed sequence.
The tadpole begins its metamorphosis in spring.
The neighborhood has undergone a complete metamorphosis.
Her metamorphosis from intern to editor took four years.

senses.head: In biology
examples: The metamorphosis from caterpillar to butterfly takes two weeks.
Insect metamorphoses follow a fixed sequence.
The tadpole begins its metamorphosis in spring.

senses.head: A dramatic change in anything
examples: The neighborhood has undergone a complete metamorphosis.
Her metamorphosis from intern to editor took four years.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the metamorphoses take weeks
entries.contrast: The stress is on the third syllable — met-uh-MOR-fuh-sis — not on -morph- alone.
